Redundancy verification of filters is performed during sea trials or commissioning by simulating a clogged condition (e.g., partially closing the inlet valve) and measuring the differential pressure rise. The standby filter must automatically or manually activate within a specified time (e.g., <10 seconds) without causing cooling water flow interruption or temperature excursion. The test confirms that the switching logic, valve actuation, and alarm system (e.g., high differential pressure alarm) function correctly per the design specification and class society requirements.

Every 2 to 6 months, a coolant sample must be sent to an independent labor- atory or to the engine manufacturer for an integrated analysis. If chemical additives or antifreeze agents are used, coolant should be re- placed after 3 years at the latest. If there is a high concentration of solids (rust) in the system, the water must be completely replaced and entire system carefully cleaned. Deposits in the cooling system may be caused by fluids that enter the coolant or by emulsion break-up, corrosion in the system, and limescale deposits if the water is very hard. If the concentration of chloride ions has increased, this generally indicates that seawater has entered the system. The maximum spe- cified concentration of 50 mg chloride ions per kg must not be exceeded as otherwise the risk of corrosion is too high.

The changeover between sea chests is performed via remotely actuated butterfly valves or gate valves, with interlocking to prevent simultaneous closure. In CCS/DNV/ABS class, the system must allow manual local operation and be designed for single-failure tolerance. Typical design practice: the standby chest is kept pressurized with a small bypass to avoid air entrapment.

After cleaning or replacement, verify filter performance by measuring the pressure drop at normal flow rate. A clean filter should show a pressure drop within 0.05-0.1 bar. If the pressure drop remains high, inspect for clogging or incorrect mesh size. Continuous monitoring via differential pressure gauges with alarm setpoints (e.g., 0.3 bar) is recommended per class requirements.

参数要求与设计惯例
For alarm system redundancy, the setpoints for primary and backup sensors should be identical to avoid hysteresis. However, a small deadband (e.g., 2% of range) may be allowed to prevent chattering during switchover. The backup channel must have independent adjustment and calibration, with tamper-proof settings. In MAN/WinGD engines, the cooling water high-temperature alarm uses dual PT100 sensors; one feeds the main alarm panel, the other the engine safety system. The switchover condition is based on sensor health status (e.g., resistance out of range) rather than process value deviation. All redundant components must be type-approved and listed in the system FMEA.

报警触发条件与设定值文件要求
The alarm system documentation must include a complete list of alarm set points and their triggering conditions, such as high temperature, low pressure, or overspeed. For each alarm, the manufacturer's manual should specify the sensor type, location, and the logic for activation (e.g., delay time, voting logic). This ensures that the alarm system can be properly calibrated and tested during commissioning and maintenance.

Corrosion is a chemical or electrochemical action that gradually wears away metal surfaces in the cooling system. In some instances, corrosion can eventually destroy an engine. All cooling system components need protection from corrosion. Supplemental coolant additives are used to protect metal surfaces. They coat these surfaces and prevent the formation of scale, rust, and cavitation erosion. Types of cooling system corrosion are pitting and cavitation erosion, rust, acidity-alkalinity imbalance caused erosion, and galvanic and electrolytic corrosion. Other functional effects of coolants with no, or low, levels of supplemental coolant additives are aeration and the formation of scale and deposits. Pitting and Cavitation-Erosion Electrical current flow in a localized area is one of the causes of pitting corrosion. Pitting is the most damaging type of corrosion.

Types of Cooling Systems There is a myriad of different types of cooling systems. No one system is correct for every location, size and application of Cat engine. It is important to work with our experienced engineers and/or the local dealer when designing the best cooling system for each application. This section discusses some of the more common types of cooling systems. There are two basic types of cooling systems, open and closed. Open System Open systems include cooling towers (without heat exchanger), spray ponds and bodies of water. Open systems are not recommended. In the open system, the cooling water is exposed directly to the air and is cooled by evaporation and water-to-air heat transfer. About 75% of the total heat is removed by evaporation, and 25% by convective heat transfer.

The switching method for redundant filters is often manual or automatic. For manual systems, a handle-operated three-way valve diverts flow to the standby filter while the clogged one is isolated for cleaning. Automatic systems use motorized valves controlled by a PLC based on differential pressure or timer. The changeover must be smooth to avoid pressure surges; a slow-closing valve or equalizing line is sometimes installed. This ensures compliance with MAN/WinGD guidelines for cooling water system reliability.

Alarm system redundancy typically adopts a 1+1 or N+1 architecture. For critical parameters (e.g., lube oil pressure, cooling water temperature), dual sensors are installed with independent power supplies and signal paths. Automatic switchover occurs when the primary sensor fails (e.g., signal out of range, short circuit, or open circuit) or during scheduled maintenance. The switchover logic is usually hardwired in the PLC or safety system, with a manual override for testing. The changeover time should be less than 1 second to avoid false alarms or loss of protection.

There are two types of cooling towers. • Open-Type • Closed-loop-Type or Evaporative Cooler Open Cooling Tower In open cooling systems using cooling towers, the engine cooling water is sprayed directly into the tower and is subjected to the inherent concentration of water contaminants of this system. Unless special provisions are made, such as a cleanable aftercooler and corrosion resistant plumbing, the use of an open cooling system is not recommended for Cat engines. Closed Cooling Tower Figure 22 demonstrates how a heat exchanger can be used to maintain a closed cooling system for the engine while using a cooling tower. In this system, raw water is circulated by an auxiliary water pump driven from the engine, or by an electric motor.
